overview.headline: Numeric geologic dating using radioactive half-life and isotopic mineral ages

keyPoints.point: Discovery of radioactivity made assignment of ages in thousands millions and billions of years possible
keyPoints.quote: The assignment of ages of rocks in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity.

keyPoints.point: Radioactive isotope half-life is length of time required for one half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms
keyPoints.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyPoints.point: Isotopic techniques measure time at which particular mineral within rock was formed to combine with fossil relative ages
keyPoints.quote: Isotopic techniques are used to measure the time at which a particular mineral within a rock was formed.

keyPoints.point: Four parent daughter decay series especially useful for dating geologic materials include carbon to nitrogen and potassium to argon
keyPoints.quote: four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful: carbon to nitrogen, potassium to argon, rubidium to strontium, and uranium to lead.

keyTerms.gloss: time required for half the parent atoms to decay at constant rate
keyTerms.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.

keyTerms.gloss: variant that differs in neutrons and naturally converts with nuclear changes
keyTerms.quote: A radioactive isotope (the parent) of one chemical element naturally converts to a stable isotope (the daughter) of another chemical element

keyTerms.gloss: discovery that enabled assigning numeric ages to rocks in millions and billions of years
keyTerms.quote: The assignment of ages of rocks in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity.

keyTerms.gloss: product of detective work to assign numeric ages to time boundaries
keyTerms.quote: To allow us to assign numeric ages to the geologic time scale

keyTerms.gloss: radioactive isotope that undergoes decay to daughter at constant rate
keyTerms.quote: four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful: carbon to nitrogen, potassium to argon, rubidium to strontium, and uranium to lead.
